narration.full_text: Today, we're diving into one of the most foundational concepts in number theory: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic. This theorem is crucial for understanding how numbers are built. At its core, the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic states that every integer greater than one is either a prime number itself, or it can be represented as a product of prime numbers. What makes this theorem so powerful is the second part: this prime factorization is unique. This means that no matter how you break down a composite number into its prime factors, you'll always end up with the exact same set of prime numbers, just possibly in a different order. For example, if we take the number twelve, we can factor it as two times six, and then six breaks down into two times three. So, twelve equals two times two times three. No other combination of prime numbers will multiply to give you twelve. This uniqueness is incredibly important and forms the basis for many other mathematical concepts, from cryptography to understanding number properties.
